concept.name: Speculator
concept.definition: In commodity futures usage, a speculator is a trader who does not hedge, but who trades with the objective of achieving profits through the successful anticipation of price movements. Speculators voluntarily accept price risk that hedgers seek to shed, thereby supplying liquidity and risk-bearing capacity to the market.
concept.intuition: A speculator is a risk-taker with a view: they have no crop to sell or fuel to buy — they simply bet on where prices are going, hoping to be paid for bearing the risk.
concept.mechanics: The speculator takes outright long or short positions (or spreads) based on anticipated price moves, posts margin, and profits or loses as prices move. Regulators monitor speculators through large-trader reporting and speculative position limits that cap the size of positions a non-hedger may hold in many futures markets.
concept.failure_modes: Speculative positioning can be crowded, so forced unwinds amplify trends and crashes; leverage plus adverse moves triggers margin spirals. At the market level, heavy one-way speculative flows can detach prices from fundamentals for extended periods.
concept.misconceptions: Speculation is not inherently manipulative or socially useless — speculators provide liquidity and assume risk hedgers want to offload. Nor is every short-term trader a speculator in the regulatory sense (e.g., bona fide hedgers are excluded from speculative limits).
concept.example: A trader with no commercial interest in crude oil buys ten WTI futures contracts expecting OPEC supply cuts to lift prices, posts initial margin, and exits two weeks later for a gain or loss.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
